scenario: Put the Linux boot sequence in order after power-on.

options.text: Firmware (UEFI/BIOS) → bootloader (GRUB 2) → kernel + initramfs → systemd → targets and services

options.note: Firmware always runs first, and the kernel starts systemd.
systemd is PID 1, started by the kernel.

explanation: After power-on, firmware (UEFI/BIOS) starts the bootloader (GRUB 2), which loads the kernel and initramfs, and the kernel then hands off to systemd, which brings up targets and services. The initramfs supplies drivers needed to mount the real root file system.

scenario: Where do you change kernel command-line defaults on a GRUB 2 system before regenerating the configuration?

options.note: grub.cfg is generated and gets overwritten.
Not used by systemd for this.

explanation: On GRUB 2 systems, edit the defaults in /etc/default/grub (GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX) and then regenerate the configuration with grub2-mkconfig or update-grub. Edits made directly to grub.cfg are overwritten the next time it is regenerated.

scenario: Which tool rebuilds the initramfs on a RHEL-family system after adding a storage driver?

options.note: Updates module dependencies but doesn't build the initramfs.

explanation: dracut builds the initramfs on RHEL-family systems; dracut -f regenerates it for the running kernel after a storage driver change. Debian uses update-initramfs. mkfs, modinfo and depmod don't build an initramfs.

scenario: Which command loads the kernel module vfio along with any modules it depends on?

options.note: insmod needs a full path and doesn't resolve dependencies.

explanation: modprobe loads a module and resolves and loads its dependencies, while insmod loads a single file with no dependency handling. modprobe -r unloads; blacklist modules in /etc/modprobe.d.

scenario: Which command lists PCI devices such as network and graphics cards, with the kernel driver in use?
explanation: lspci lists PCI devices, and -k adds the kernel driver in use and available modules. lsusb handles USB, lscpu the CPU, and dmidecode reads firmware (DMI) tables.

scenario: You add a new 20 GiB disk /dev/sdb for a database. Which order creates an LVM volume ready to mount?

options.text: pvcreate /dev/sdb → vgcreate vgdata /dev/sdb → lvcreate -n lvdb -L 15G vgdata → mkfs.xfs /dev/vgdata/lvdb

options.note: Formatting first would be overwritten by pvcreate.

explanation: LVM is built bottom-up: pvcreate on the disk, vgcreate to make a volume group, lvcreate for the logical volume, then mkfs and mount. Putting a file system on the raw disk first would prevent using it as a physical volume.

scenario: Which command grows logical volume lvweb by 5 GiB and resizes its file system in one step?

options.note: Sets an absolute size of 5G instead of adding 5G, and doesn't resize the file system.

explanation: lvextend -r -L +5G grows the LV and, with -r, also resizes the file system using the right tool (xfs_growfs for XFS, resize2fs for ext4). +5G adds 5 GiB while 5G sets an absolute size, and without -r the file system stays the old size.

scenario: Which file system can be grown but not shrunk?

options.note: tmpfs is memory-based and resizable with remount.

explanation: XFS can be grown while mounted (xfs_growfs) but cannot be shrunk; ext4 can be both grown and shrunk, with the file system unmounted for shrinking. XFS is the RHEL default.

scenario: Which /etc/fstab entry mounts an XFS volume by UUID at /data at boot?

options.note: Device comes first, then mount point.
That's a command, not an fstab line.

explanation: An fstab line has six fields in order: device, mount point, type, options, dump and fsck order, so UUID=... /data xfs defaults 0 0 is correct. Find UUIDs with blkid or lsblk -f and test with mount -a before rebooting.

scenario: Which mount option prevents programs on a mounted file system from being executed?

options.note: nosuid ignores SUID/SGID bits but still allows execution.
Read-only, but binaries can still run.

explanation: noexec stops binaries on that file system from being run directly. nosuid ignores setuid bits, nodev ignores device files and ro makes it read-only. Hardening /tmp commonly uses nodev,nosuid,noexec.

scenario: A disk reports free space, but writes fail with "No space left on device." Which command confirms inode exhaustion?
explanation: When writes fail with 'No space left on device' but df -h shows free space, check inodes with df -i. Millions of small files can exhaust the inode table even though blocks remain free.

scenario: Which command creates a RAID 1 array from /dev/sdb1 and /dev/sdc1?

options.note: --assemble starts existing arrays, and level 0 is striping.

explanation: mdadm --create builds the array; --level=1 is a mirror with two devices. Watch the status in /proc/mdstat or mdadm --detail. RAID 5 stripes with parity and RAID 10 mirrors then stripes; --assemble only reactivates existing arrays.

scenario: Which /etc/fstab entry mounts an NFS export from nas01?
explanation: An NFS entry in fstab uses server:/export as the device, the nfs type and _netdev so mounting waits for the network. The //server/share form is for SMB/CIFS.

scenario: Which tmpfs property matters when you mount /tmp as tmpfs?

options.text: Contents live in RAM (and swap) and disappear at reboot
It can't have a size limit

explanation: tmpfs keeps its contents in RAM (and swap), so everything disappears at reboot, and you can cap it with size=. It is fast and needs no partition.

scenario: Which command shows NetworkManager connection profiles and their devices?
explanation: nmcli connection show lists NetworkManager connection profiles and their devices. Change one with nmcli con mod and activate it with nmcli con up. netplan and ifconfig aren't NetworkManager tools.

scenario: On Ubuntu Server, where is the network configuration usually defined?

options.text: YAML files in /etc/netplan, applied with netplan apply

explanation: Ubuntu Server defines networking in YAML files under /etc/netplan, applied with netplan apply. netplan try rolls back automatically if connectivity is lost. /etc/sysconfig/network-scripts is the older RHEL layout.

scenario: Which file controls whether the system checks /etc/hosts before DNS?

options.note: Lists DNS servers and search domains.

explanation: /etc/nsswitch.conf controls lookup order; with hosts: files dns, a matching /etc/hosts entry wins before DNS is queried. resolv.conf only lists DNS servers.

scenario: Which shell startup file is the right place for a user's personal aliases in Bash interactive shells?
explanation: Personal aliases for interactive Bash shells belong in ~/.bashrc. Login shells read /etc/profile and ~/.bash_profile, which usually sources ~/.bashrc, and system-wide snippets go in /etc/profile.d.

scenario: In vim, how do you save changes and quit?

options.text: Press Esc, then type :wq and press Enter

options.note: Not vim keys; Ctrl+S can freeze terminal output.

explanation: In vim, press Esc to leave insert mode and type :wq then Enter to write and quit. :q! quits without saving; Ctrl+S and Ctrl+X are not vim commands.

scenario: Which command makes a compressed, permission-preserving archive of /etc?

options.note: dd copies devices or files byte by byte.

explanation: tar -czpf creates a gzip-compressed archive and -p preserves permissions. cp -r doesn't compress, gzip -r compresses files individually and dd copies raw blocks.

scenario: Which command copies only changed files from /srv/www to a backup server and preserves attributes?
explanation: rsync -a copies recursively while preserving attributes and transfers only changed files; --delete mirrors deletions, and the trailing slash on the source copies the directory's contents. scp -r recopies everything.

scenario: Which tool makes an exact block-level image of a disk, including empty space?
explanation: dd copies raw blocks, so the image includes partitions, boot data and unused space, for example dd if=/dev/sdb of=sdb.img bs=4M status=progress. rsync and tar copy files, not blocks. ddrescue is better for failing disks.

scenario: Which pair describes KVM and QEMU?

options.text: KVM is the kernel's hardware virtualization module; QEMU emulates the devices and runs the VM
KVM is a container runtime; QEMU is a firewall
QEMU is the kernel module; KVM is a GUI

explanation: KVM is the kernel's hardware virtualization module and QEMU emulates devices and runs the VM; libvirt manages them with virsh or virt-manager. KVM is not a container runtime.

scenario: Which command lists all virtual machines managed by libvirt, including stopped ones?
explanation: virsh list --all shows every libvirt domain, including those that are shut off. Plain virsh list shows only running ones.

scenario: Which VM disk format supports thin provisioning and snapshots in QEMU?

options.note: Raw is simple and fast but has no built-in snapshots.
A file system, not an image format.

explanation: qcow2 is QEMU's copy-on-write image format with thin provisioning and snapshot support (qemu-img create -f qcow2). Raw images have neither.

scenario: What does nested virtualization allow?

options.text: Running a hypervisor inside a virtual machine
Running two OSes on one disk partition
Sharing one VM between two hosts

explanation: Nested virtualization lets a hypervisor run inside a virtual machine, useful for labs and CI. It requires CPU virtualization support to be exposed to the VM.

scenario: Which statement describes RPM-based versus dpkg-based distributions?

options.text: RHEL, Fedora, and SUSE use RPM packages; Debian and Ubuntu use .deb packages managed by dpkg/apt
Both families use the same package format

options.note: RPM is used on servers widely.

explanation: RHEL, Fedora and SUSE use RPM packages (dnf/yum, zypper), while Debian and Ubuntu use .deb packages managed by dpkg and apt. dpkg isn't used by RHEL.

scenario: Which directory in the FHS contains kernel and process information as virtual files?
explanation: /proc is a virtual file system exposing kernel and process information; /sys exposes devices and drivers, /dev holds device nodes and /run holds runtime data. /var and /opt are real storage.

scenario: Which display server protocol is the modern replacement for X11 on most desktop distributions?
explanation: Wayland is the modern display protocol replacing X11 on most distributions. GDM, SDDM and LightDM are display managers for graphical login, and GNOME is a desktop environment.

scenario: Which CPU architecture name refers to 64-bit ARM?
explanation: AArch64 (arm64) is the 64-bit ARM architecture; x86_64 is 64-bit Intel/AMD and i686 is 32-bit x86. Check yours with uname -m or lscpu.

scenario: What does PXE boot do?

options.text: Boots a computer over the network from a server, often to start an automated installation

explanation: PXE boots a computer over the network (DHCP plus TFTP or HTTP) and is often combined with Kickstart or cloud-init for unattended installs. It isn't a USB boot or disk encryption.

scenario: Which command shows how much disk space each subdirectory of /var uses?

options.note: Shows only top-level file block counts.

explanation: du -sh /var/* shows the total size of each subdirectory; pipe to sort -h to rank them. df reports file system usage, not directory sizes.

scenario: Which command checks and repairs an unmounted ext4 file system?
explanation: fsck.ext4 (e2fsck) checks and repairs an unmounted ext4 file system; never run it on a mounted one. XFS uses xfs_repair instead.

scenario: Which environment variable sets the default editor that tools like crontab -e and visudo use?
explanation: EDITOR (or VISUAL) names the default editor used by crontab -e and visudo; set it with export EDITOR=vim in ~/.bashrc. PATH and SHELL don't select editors.

scenario: Which command creates the service account svcbackup with no login shell and no home directory?

options.note: Creates a regular user with a home.
Creates a group, not a user.

explanation: useradd -r creates a system account with a low UID, -s /sbin/nologin denies interactive login and -M skips the home directory. Service accounts shouldn't have shells.

scenario: Which command forces user dana to change her password at next login?

options.note: -E sets the account expiry date; 0 expires the account.

explanation: chage -d 0 sets the last password change to the epoch, so the user must set a new password at next login. -E sets the account expiry, and passwd -l only locks the password.

scenario: Which command locks the account of a user who left the company without deleting files?
explanation: usermod -L (or passwd -l) locks the password, preserving files, but SSH key logins can still work, so also expire the account with chage -E 0. userdel -r would delete the home directory.

scenario: Which directory provides template files copied into each new user's home directory?
explanation: Files in /etc/skel are copied into each new home directory, so a standard .bashrc or README placed there reaches every user created with useradd -m.

scenario: Which file stores password hashes and aging information?

options.note: Account fields only; x placeholder for password.

explanation: /etc/shadow holds password hashes and aging information and is readable only by root. /etc/passwd has no hashes, and login.defs holds defaults.

scenario: What is a process's PPID?

options.text: The process ID of its parent process

explanation: PPID is the process ID of the parent process. ps -ef shows PID and PPID and pstree shows the tree. It's not a priority or a port.

scenario: In ps output, what does process state Z mean?

options.text: Zombie: it has exited but its parent hasn't collected its exit status

explanation: State Z is a zombie: the process has exited but its parent hasn't collected its exit status. It uses no CPU or memory but occupies a PID; fix or restart the parent.

scenario: Which command lowers the priority of the running process 2211 to nice value 10?
explanation: renice -n 10 -p 2211 changes the priority of a running process. Nice ranges from -20 (highest priority) to 19 (lowest), and only root can lower a value. nice only starts new commands.

scenario: You started a long command in the foreground. How do you move it to the background?

options.text: Press Ctrl+Z to suspend it, then run bg

options.note: & works only when starting the command.
fg brings jobs to the foreground.

explanation: Press Ctrl+Z to suspend the foreground job, then run bg to continue it in the background; jobs lists jobs and fg resumes. Ctrl+C would terminate it, and nohup keeps it alive after logout.

scenario: Which signal does kill send by default?
explanation: kill sends SIGTERM (15) by default, letting the program clean up. SIGKILL (9) can't be caught, SIGHUP (1) often means reread config and SIGINT (2) is Ctrl+C.

scenario: Which crontab line runs /usr/local/bin/report.sh at 2:30 AM every weekday?

options.note: 1-5 there means days of the month.

explanation: Crontab fields are minute, hour, day-of-month, month, day-of-week, so 30 2 * * 1-5 runs at 2:30 AM Monday through Friday. Edit with crontab -e.

scenario: A laptop is often off at night. Which tool ensures daily maintenance jobs still run after it boots?

options.note: Skips jobs missed while powered off.

explanation: anacron runs daily, weekly and monthly jobs that were missed while a machine was off, which suits laptops. systemd timers can do the same with Persistent=true; cron skips missed runs.

scenario: Which command schedules a one-time job to run at 11 PM tonight?
explanation: at schedules a one-time job, for example echo "script" | at 23:00. atq lists pending jobs and atrm removes them; cron is for repeating jobs.

scenario: Which command imports a repository's GPG key on a RHEL-family system?
explanation: rpm --import adds a repository's GPG key on RHEL-family systems, and repos set gpgcheck=1 with a gpgkey= URL. Debian-family systems use signed-by keyrings rather than apt-key.

scenario: Which command shows which package provides /usr/bin/dig on a RHEL system?
explanation: dnf provides /usr/bin/dig finds which package supplies a file, even if it isn't installed. rpm -qf /path works for installed files and dpkg -S is the Debian equivalent.

scenario: Several versions of Java are installed. Which tool switches the system default java command?

options.note: Works but bypasses the managed system.

explanation: update-alternatives (alternatives on RHEL) manages symlinks for commands with several installed versions; --config java lets you choose the default.

scenario: Which systemd unit type runs a service on a schedule, similar to cron?
explanation: A .timer unit triggers a matching .service on a schedule, similar to cron, with OnCalendar= and Persistent=true to run missed jobs. List them with systemctl list-timers.

scenario: You edited a unit file in /etc/systemd/system. What must you run before restarting the service?
explanation: After editing a unit file, run systemctl daemon-reload so systemd rereads it before you restart the service. systemctl edit creates drop-ins and reloads automatically.

refs.title: systemctl - Control the systemd system and service manager

scenario: What does systemctl mask httpd do?

options.text: Links the unit to /dev/null so it can't be started, even manually or as a dependency

explanation: systemctl mask links the unit to /dev/null so it can't be started, even manually or as a dependency; unmask undoes it. disable only stops it starting at boot.

refs.title: systemctl - Control the systemd system and service manager

scenario: Which command shows how long each unit took during the last boot?
explanation: systemd-analyze blame lists how long each unit took to start at the last boot, and critical-chain shows the slowest dependency chain.

scenario: Which command sets the system time zone to America/New_York?
explanation: timedatectl set-timezone America/New_York sets the time zone, and timedatectl also shows NTP synchronization status. Time sync is handled by chronyd or systemd-timesyncd.

scenario: Which command permanently sets the hostname to web01.example.com?
explanation: hostnamectl set-hostname makes the change permanent by writing /etc/hostname. The hostname command alone changes it only until reboot, and /etc/hosts maps names to addresses.

scenario: Which command lists DNS servers in use per interface on a system running systemd-resolved?
explanation: resolvectl status shows the DNS servers per interface on systems running systemd-resolved, where /etc/resolv.conf points to the stub resolver 127.0.0.53.

refs.title: resolvectl - Query and configure the systemd-resolved DNS resolver

scenario: Which command runs an NGINX container in the background, maps host port 8080 to container port 80, and names it web?

options.note: Ports are host:container, so this maps host 80 to container 8080.
exec runs a command in a running container.

explanation: podman run -d --name web -p 8080:80 runs detached, names the container and maps host port 8080 to container port 80 (host:container). Reversing the ports would expose the wrong one.

scenario: How do you keep a container's data after the container is removed?

options.text: Store it in a volume or bind mount, such as -v webdata:/usr/share/nginx/html

explanation: Container filesystems are discarded when the container is removed, so persist data in a named volume or bind mount (-v). On SELinux hosts add :Z to relabel bind mounts.

scenario: In a Dockerfile/Containerfile, which instruction sets the base image?
explanation: FROM sets the base image in a Containerfile or Dockerfile; each following instruction (RUN, COPY and so on) creates a layer. CMD defines the default command.

scenario: What is a rootless container?

options.text: A container started by an unprivileged user, so a breakout doesn't grant root on the host
A container with no file system
A container that runs only as root

explanation: A rootless container runs under an unprivileged user (via user namespaces), so a breakout doesn't give root on the host. Podman does this by default for regular users.

scenario: Which command shows the logs of the container named api?

options.note: Container logs are managed by the runtime.

explanation: podman logs api shows the container's output (add -f to follow). podman inspect shows configuration such as mounts, ports and IP, not logs.

scenario: Which configuration file defines virtual hosts for the Apache web server on RHEL?
explanation: On RHEL, Apache (httpd) reads every *.conf file in /etc/httpd/conf.d, so virtual hosts normally go there. Debian-family Apache uses /etc/apache2/sites-available with a2ensite. Test with apachectl configtest.

scenario: Which service hands out IP addresses to clients on a network?

options.text: A DHCP server (such as Kea or ISC dhcpd)

explanation: A DHCP server (Kea or ISC dhcpd) leases IP addresses, gateways and DNS settings to clients. SMTP sends mail, IMAP lets clients read it, and NTP synchronizes time.

scenario: Which statement describes PTP compared with NTP?

options.text: PTP provides much more precise (sub-microsecond) synchronization, often with hardware timestamping
PTP is an older, less accurate NTP
PTP only works over the internet

explanation: PTP provides far more precise synchronization (sub-microsecond, often with hardware timestamping) than NTP. Linux uses linuxptp (ptp4l) for PTP and chrony for NTP.

scenario: What is the safest way to give the ops group permission to restart nginx with sudo?

options.text: Add a file in /etc/sudoers.d edited with visudo -f, such as %ops ALL=(root) /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx
Add ops to the wheel group

options.note: A syntax error can lock out sudo.

options.text: Share the root password with ops

explanation: Grant only the needed command with a drop-in in /etc/sudoers.d edited via visudo -f, for example %ops ALL=(root) /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx. That's least privilege; visudo checks the syntax before saving, and wheel or the root password give far more.

scenario: Which command makes a log file append-only, even for root, until the attribute is removed?

options.note: Ownership doesn't prevent edits by root.

explanation: chattr +a makes a file append-only even for root until removed; +i makes it immutable. View attributes with lsattr. chmod and chown can't do this.

scenario: With umask 027, what permissions does a newly created file get?

options.note: Files don't get execute by default.

explanation: Files start at 666 and directories at 777, then the umask bits are removed: 666 minus 027 gives 640 (rw-r-----) and directories get 750.

scenario: Which command gives user maria read access to report.csv without changing its owner, group, or mode?
explanation: setfacl -m u:maria:r adds a user ACL entry without changing the owner, group or mode. getfacl displays ACLs, a + in ls -l indicates one, and default ACLs (-d) apply to new files in a directory.

scenario: Which SSH server settings reduce risk on an internet-facing server?

options.text: PermitRootLogin no and PasswordAuthentication no (keys only)

options.note: Telnet's port; changing ports isn't real security.

explanation: Setting PermitRootLogin no and PasswordAuthentication no leaves only key logins for normal users. Validate with sshd -t and add AllowUsers or AllowGroups to restrict who can log in.

scenario: Which protocols should be replaced because they send credentials in clear text?

options.text: Telnet, FTP, and HTTP for logins

explanation: Telnet, FTP and plain HTTP send credentials in clear text and should be replaced with SSH, SFTP/SCP, HTTPS and TLS-protected mail protocols.

scenario: What does Secure Boot do?

options.text: Verifies that the bootloader and kernel are signed by trusted keys before running them

explanation: Secure Boot verifies that the bootloader and kernel are signed by trusted keys before they run; shim and GRUB are signed, and mokutil manages extra keys. It doesn't encrypt the disk.

scenario: Which framework lets you require MFA or enforce password complexity for Linux logins?
explanation: PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules) governs authentication, configured in /etc/pam.d. pam_pwquality enforces password rules and pam_faillock locks accounts after failed attempts; SELinux and auditd do different jobs.

scenario: Which service lets Linux hosts authenticate users against Active Directory or LDAP and cache credentials?
explanation: SSSD connects Linux to Active Directory or LDAP and caches credentials; join a domain with realm join. Kerberos provides ticket-based authentication, and Winbind is the Samba alternative.

scenario: What does polkit control?

options.text: Whether unprivileged processes may perform system actions, such as a desktop user mounting a disk

options.note: That's PAM and the crypto library.

explanation: polkit decides whether unprivileged processes may perform privileged system actions, such as a desktop user mounting a disk; pkexec runs a command as another user under polkit rules.

scenario: Which tool records security-relevant events such as changes to /etc/passwd, using rules like -w /etc/passwd -p wa?
explanation: auditd records security-relevant events, such as writes or attribute changes to /etc/passwd from a rule like -w /etc/passwd -p wa. Search with ausearch and summarize with aureport.

scenario: Which tool rotates, compresses, and deletes old log files on a schedule?
explanation: logrotate rotates, compresses and deletes old logs on a schedule, configured in /etc/logrotate.conf and /etc/logrotate.d. The systemd journal's size is limited in journald.conf.

scenario: Which command permanently allows HTTPS through firewalld and applies it immediately?

options.note: Runtime only; lost at reload or reboot.
ufw rules are already persistent, and it's a different tool.

explanation: firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=https writes the rule to the saved configuration and --reload applies it. Without --permanent the rule disappears on reload or reboot.

scenario: On Ubuntu with ufw, which commands deny all inbound traffic except SSH?

options.text: ufw default deny incoming, ufw allow OpenSSH, then ufw enable
ufw enable, then ufw allow all

explanation: On Ubuntu with ufw, set the default to deny incoming, allow OpenSSH, and then enable ufw. Allow SSH first or you will lock yourself out of a remote server.

scenario: Which tool is the modern kernel packet-filtering framework that replaces iptables?

options.note: Stores sets of addresses for iptables/nftables.

explanation: nftables (nft) is the modern kernel packet-filtering framework replacing iptables, and firewalld uses it as its back end on current distributions.

scenario: What is the difference between stateful and stateless filtering?

options.text: Stateful firewalls track connections and allow return traffic automatically; stateless rules check each packet alone
Stateless firewalls are always more secure

explanation: A stateful firewall tracks connections (conntrack) and allows return traffic for established flows, while stateless filtering judges each packet on its own. Stateful is the Linux norm, for example ct state established,related accept.

scenario: A Linux host must route traffic between two networks. Which setting must be enabled?
explanation: Routing between networks requires IP forwarding: net.ipv4.ip_forward=1, persisted in /etc/sysctl.d. Add masquerade (source NAT) so private hosts can reach the internet through the router.

scenario: Which command encrypts a whole partition with LUKS2?

options.note: Encrypts a file, not a block device for use.

explanation: cryptsetup luksFormat encrypts a partition with LUKS; then cryptsetup open it, create a file system on /dev/mapper/name, and list it in /etc/crypttab. gpg and openssl encrypt files, not block devices.

scenario: Which command checks the expiry date of a server certificate file?
explanation: openssl x509 -in server.crt -noout -enddate prints a certificate's expiry date, and openssl s_client -connect host:443 tests a live TLS connection and shows the chain.

scenario: Which TLS versions should a hardened Linux server allow?
explanation: A hardened server should allow only TLS 1.2 and 1.3; SSLv3 and TLS 1.0/1.1 are deprecated. On RHEL, system-wide crypto policies (update-crypto-policies) remove weak algorithms.

scenario: Which hash function is appropriate for verifying a downloaded ISO's integrity?
explanation: Use SHA-256 (sha256sum) to verify a download against the publisher's signed checksum. MD5 and SHA-1 are no longer collision-resistant, and Base64 and ROT13 aren't hashes.

scenario: WireGuard is best described as what?

options.text: A simple, modern VPN built into the Linux kernel

explanation: WireGuard is a simple, modern VPN built into the Linux kernel, configured with wg and wg-quick, where peers exchange public keys. It is not a firewall or an IDS.

refs.title: WireGuard: fast, modern, secure VPN tunnel

scenario: Which control blocks a user after five failed login attempts on modern RHEL and Ubuntu?

options.note: pam_tally2 is deprecated/removed on current distributions.

explanation: pam_faillock locks an account after repeated failed logins (configure /etc/security/faillock.conf); faillock --user shows and resets failures. pam_tally2 is the older module.

scenario: Which tool scans a system against a security profile such as a CIS Benchmark and produces a report?
explanation: OpenSCAP (oscap) evaluates a system against a security profile such as a CIS Benchmark and produces a report. AIDE detects changed files by comparing hashes to a baseline, and nmap scans networks.

scenario: Which value in a vulnerability report rates its severity on a 0–10 scale?
explanation: CVSS rates a vulnerability's severity on a 0-10 scale. A CVE is just an identifier, and CWE classifies weakness types. Patch high and critical findings first.

scenario: How should you securely wipe a decommissioned hard disk?

options.text: Use a verified method such as shred or the drive's secure-erase command, or physically destroy it

explanation: Securely wipe disks with shred or the drive's secure-erase command, or physically destroy them. For SSDs use the manufacturer's secure or crypto erase, because overwriting may miss remapped blocks; deleting partitions or reformatting leaves data.

scenario: What does SELinux in enforcing mode do?

options.text: Applies mandatory access control policy and blocks actions the policy doesn't allow, even for root-owned processes

explanation: In enforcing mode SELinux applies mandatory access control and blocks actions the policy doesn't allow, even for root-owned processes. Permissive only logs; getenforce shows the mode, and Ubuntu and SUSE use AppArmor instead.

scenario: What is the purpose of a login banner in /etc/issue.net and sshd's Banner setting?

options.text: To display an authorized-use warning before login, supporting legal and compliance requirements

explanation: A login banner (/etc/issue.net with sshd's Banner) shows an authorized-use warning before login, supporting legal and compliance needs. /etc/motd shows a message after login.

scenario: What does idempotent mean in configuration management tools such as Ansible?

options.text: Running the same task again leaves the system in the same state without making extra changes
A task runs only once ever
options.note: It can run many times safely.

explanation: Idempotent means running a task again leaves the system in the same state without extra changes. Ansible modules check state first and report 'changed' only when they act.

scenario: Which statement contrasts Ansible and Puppet?

options.text: Ansible pushes changes over SSH without an agent; Puppet agents pull configuration from a server

explanation: Ansible is agentless: the control node pushes changes over SSH using YAML playbooks. Puppet agents pull configuration from a server written in its own declarative language.

scenario: In an Ansible playbook, what defines which machines a play runs against?

options.text: The hosts line, matching groups or hosts in the inventory

explanation: The hosts line of a play selects which inventory hosts or groups it runs against, for example ansible-playbook -i inventory site.yml. Tasks define what runs and handlers run once at the end when notified.

scenario: What is infrastructure as code (IaC)?

options.text: Defining servers, networks, and settings in version-controlled files that tools apply automatically
Writing code on servers by hand

explanation: Infrastructure as code defines servers, networks and settings in version-controlled files applied by tools, so changes are reviewed and repeatable. OpenTofu/Terraform provision and Ansible configures.

scenario: Which file automates an unattended RHEL installation?

options.note: Configures cloud instances at first boot, not the installer.

explanation: A Kickstart file (ks.cfg) automates unattended RHEL installs; pass it with inst.ks= on the boot line or embed it in the ISO. cloud-init user-data configures cloud instances instead.

scenario: What does cloud-init do?

options.text: Configures a cloud instance at first boot: hostname, users, SSH keys, packages, and scripts from user-data

explanation: cloud-init configures a cloud instance at first boot from user-data (often YAML beginning #cloud-config): hostname, users, SSH keys, packages and scripts.

scenario: Which tool runs multiple related containers from a YAML file, such as a web app with its database?
explanation: Docker Compose or Podman Compose runs several related containers from one YAML file. Kubernetes and Swarm orchestrate containers across many hosts with scaling and self-healing.

scenario: In a CI/CD pipeline, what does continuous integration mean?

options.text: Every code change is automatically built and tested when it's merged

explanation: Continuous integration means every code change is built and tested automatically when merged. Continuous delivery or deployment then releases tested builds.

scenario: In Bash, what does "${name:-guest}" expand to when name is unset or empty?

options.note: The variable's value would be used if set.

explanation: ${name:-guest} expands to 'guest' when name is unset or empty, and to the value otherwise. ${#var} gives length and ${var%.txt} strips a suffix.

scenario: Which line is a correct Bash function definition?
explanation: A Bash function is defined as name() { commands; }, and called by name with its own $1, $2. return sets its status. def and => belong to other languages.

scenario: Which loop reads a file line by line safely?

options.text: while IFS= read -r line; do echo "$line"; done < hosts.txt

options.note: Loops over the single word hosts.txt.

explanation: while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done < file reads a file line by line safely: IFS= preserves leading spaces and -r keeps backslashes. A for loop would split on whitespace.

scenario: Which test checks if the number in $count is greater than 10?
explanation: Use [ "$count" -gt 10 ] for numeric comparison in test brackets. A bare > redirects output, and (( count > 10 )) is the arithmetic form.

scenario: What does a case statement do in a Bash script?

options.text: Matches a value against patterns and runs the commands for the first match
Loops a fixed number of times

explanation: A case statement matches a value against patterns and runs the commands of the first match, ending each branch with ;; and the block with esac.

scenario: Which command prints the third field of each line in a comma-separated file?
explanation: awk -F, '{print $3}' sets comma as the field separator and prints the third field; OFS controls the output separator. cut -f3 would use tab as the delimiter.

scenario: Which Python practice keeps a project's dependencies isolated from the system Python?

options.text: Create a virtual environment with python3 -m venv .venv and install packages into it

explanation: Create a virtual environment with python3 -m venv .venv and install packages into it, recording dependencies in requirements.txt. Using sudo pip alters the system Python and risks breaking system tools.

scenario: Which Python data type is an ordered, changeable collection like ["web01", "web02"]?
explanation: A list is ordered and mutable, a tuple is ordered but immutable, a set is unordered and a dict holds key-value pairs. Common admin modules include os, subprocess, pathlib, json, argparse and logging.

scenario: Which git command creates a new branch named fix-login and switches to it?

options.text: git switch -c fix-login (or git checkout -b fix-login)

explanation: git switch -c fix-login (or git checkout -b) creates a branch and switches to it. git branch -d deletes a branch and git merge combines branches.

scenario: What is the difference between git merge and git rebase?

options.text: Merge combines histories with a merge commit; rebase replays your commits on top of another branch for a linear history

explanation: Merge combines histories with a merge commit; rebase replays your commits on top of another branch for a linear history. Avoid rebasing commits others have already pulled.

scenario: What does git stash do?

options.text: Saves uncommitted changes temporarily and cleans the working tree

explanation: git stash saves uncommitted changes temporarily and cleans the working tree; restore them with git stash pop. It doesn't push or tag.

scenario: Which file tells git not to track build output and secrets such as .env?
explanation: .gitignore lists files git should not track, such as build output and .env secrets. Never commit credentials; if you do, rotate them.

scenario: Which is a responsible practice when using an AI assistant to write a shell script for production?

options.text: Review and test the output in a non-production environment, and never paste secrets or confidential data into the prompt
Assume it's correct because it's well formatted
Include real passwords so it works

explanation: AI-generated scripts must be reviewed and tested outside production, and secrets or confidential data should never go in prompts. A well-formatted answer isn't necessarily correct, and company AI and data policies apply.

scenario: In monitoring, what is an SLO?

options.text: A target value for a service-level indicator, such as 99.9% of requests succeeding each month

explanation: An SLO is a target for a service-level indicator, such as 99.9% of requests succeeding each month. SLIs are the measurements and SLAs are customer agreements with consequences.

scenario: Which statement describes agentless monitoring?

options.text: The monitoring server polls hosts with existing protocols such as SNMP or SSH instead of installing software on them
Each host runs a monitoring agent

explanation: Agentless monitoring polls hosts with existing protocols (SNMP, SSH) instead of installing software on them. Agents gather richer metrics but add deployment work.

scenario: What does this script line do? set -euo pipefail

options.text: Exits on errors and unset variables, and fails a pipeline if any command in it fails

explanation: set -euo pipefail makes a script exit on errors (-e), treat unset variables as errors (-u) and fail a pipeline if any command in it fails (pipefail). It's a common safe default, not debugging or root.

scenario: Which regular expression matches an IPv4-like pattern of four groups of 1–3 digits separated by dots (grep -E)?

options.note: Matches only two groups, and . is unescaped.
Three digits only; \d isn't supported by grep -E.

explanation: ([0-9]{1,3}\.){3}[0-9]{1,3} matches four groups of 1-3 digits separated by escaped dots. It doesn't validate ranges (999 matches) but works for pulling addresses from logs; an unescaped . matches any character.

scenario: After adding a line to /etc/fstab, a server drops to emergency mode at boot. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The fstab entry has a typo, wrong UUID, or a device that isn't present

explanation: A typo, wrong UUID or absent device in a new fstab line makes the boot hang or drop to emergency mode. Fix the entry (or add nofail for optional devices), run systemctl daemon-reload and always test with mount -a before rebooting.

scenario: The root file system is 100% full. Which command finds the largest directories under /var?

options.note: df shows totals per file system.

explanation: du -xh /var | sort -h | tail finds the largest directories without crossing file systems. Logs, the journal, package caches and core dumps are common culprits, and lsof +L1 reveals deleted files still held open.

scenario: df shows a full disk, but du can't find the files. What is a likely explanation?

options.text: A process still holds a deleted file open, so its space isn't freed

explanation: When df shows a full disk but du can't find the files, a process is still holding a deleted file open, so its space isn't freed. Restart the process or truncate the file via /proc/<pid>/fd.

scenario: A service fails to start. Which commands show why?

options.text: systemctl status app and journalctl -u app -b

explanation: systemctl status app shows the unit state and recent log lines, and journalctl -u app -b shows this boot's full log. Look for exit codes, missing files, permission errors and SELinux denials.

refs.title: systemctl - Control the systemd system and service manager

scenario: The kernel panics during boot after an update. What is the quickest recovery?

options.text: Select the previous kernel from the GRUB menu, then investigate or remove the faulty one

explanation: If a new kernel panics, pick the previous kernel from the GRUB menu, then investigate or remove the faulty one. Set the default with grubby --set-default; reinstalling the OS is far too drastic.

scenario: A user's quota is exceeded. Which command reports their usage and limits?

options.text: quota -u username (or repquota for all users)

explanation: quota -u username shows a user's usage and limits, and repquota reports all users. Quotas are enabled with usrquota mount options and managed with edquota or xfs_quota.

scenario: A process keeps using more memory until the system kills it. What is this called and which component killed it?

options.text: A memory leak; the kernel's OOM killer ended it
A zombie process; systemd killed it
A race condition; SELinux killed it

explanation: A process whose memory grows without bound has a memory leak, and when memory runs out the kernel's OOM killer ends it, logging 'Out of memory: Killed process' in dmesg or journalctl -k.

scenario: A host can reach other hosts by IP address but not by name. What should you check first?

options.text: DNS settings: /etc/resolv.conf or resolvectl, and test with dig or getent hosts

explanation: If hosts respond by IP but not by name, it's a name-resolution problem: check /etc/resolv.conf or resolvectl, /etc/hosts and nsswitch order, and test with dig or getent hosts.

scenario: A server can reach hosts on its own subnet but nothing beyond it. What is the most likely issue?

options.text: A missing or wrong default gateway (check ip route)

options.note: Names fail, but IP to remote hosts would work.

explanation: Reaching only the local subnet points to a missing or wrong default gateway; check ip route and fix it with nmcli con mod ipv4.gateway and reactivate the connection. DNS issues would still allow IP access.

scenario: Small packets work, but large transfers over a VPN stall. What should you suspect?

options.text: An MTU mismatch; test with ping -M do -s 1400 and lower the MTU if needed

explanation: Small packets work but large VPN transfers stall: suspect an MTU mismatch, since tunnels add headers. Test with ping -M do -s 1400 and lower the MTU if needed.

scenario: Two hosts report "duplicate address detected" or intermittent connectivity. What tool helps confirm an IP conflict?

options.text: arping -D (or check ip neigh for changing MAC addresses)

explanation: For a suspected duplicate IP, run arping -D (duplicate address detection) or watch ip neigh for a changing MAC address; then find the owner in switch or DHCP records.

scenario: A web server works locally (curl localhost), but clients can't connect. Which two causes are most likely on RHEL?

options.text: firewalld isn't allowing the port, or the service is listening only on 127.0.0.1

options.note: Clients connect by IP or name; local works.

explanation: If curl localhost works but clients can't connect, either firewalld doesn't allow the port or the service listens only on 127.0.0.1. Check ss -tlnp for the listening address and firewall-cmd --list-all.

scenario: Which command shows the path packets take to a remote host and where they stop?
explanation: traceroute (or tracepath/mtr) shows each hop packets take and where they stop; mtr combines ping and traceroute with per-hop loss.

scenario: Which tool captures packets on eth0 to analyze a network problem?
explanation: tcpdump -i eth0 captures packets on that interface; save with -w capture.pcap and analyze in Wireshark.

scenario: Apache can't read files in /srv/web, although the Unix permissions are correct and SELinux is enforcing. What fixes it?

options.text: Label the content: semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/srv/web(/.*)?" then restorecon -Rv /srv/web

options.note: Permissions aren't the problem and 777 is unsafe.

explanation: When Unix permissions are right but SELinux blocks Apache, label the content: semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/srv/web(/.*)?" then restorecon -Rv. Don't use chmod 777 or disable SELinux; find denials with ausearch -m avc.

scenario: A user gets "Permission denied" on /srv/share/plan.txt, which is mode 660, group projects. The user was just added to projects. Why?

options.text: Group membership applies at login; the user must log out and back in (or use newgrp)

explanation: Group membership is read at login, so a user just added to projects must log out and back in (or use newgrp) before it applies. Check with id, and also parent directory execute permission and ACLs.

scenario: A user can't log in, and passwd -S shows L. What does it mean?

options.text: Login is allowed only by key

explanation: In passwd -S output, L means the password is locked. Unlock with usermod -U or passwd -u, and also check chage -l for expiry, faillock, and the shell (nologin).

scenario: Browsers show a certificate error for an internal site. The certificate is valid. What is a common cause?

options.text: The server isn't sending the intermediate certificate chain, or the name doesn't match the certificate

explanation: A valid certificate can still fail in browsers if the server doesn't send the intermediate chain or the name doesn't match. openssl s_client -connect site:443 -showcerts shows what is sent.

scenario: A scan reports an SSH server offering weak ciphers. Where do you fix it on RHEL?

options.text: Apply a stricter system crypto policy (update-crypto-policies) or set Ciphers/KexAlgorithms in sshd configuration
Remove the host keys and restart

explanation: Weak SSH ciphers are fixed by a stricter system crypto policy (update-crypto-policies) or by setting Ciphers and KexAlgorithms in sshd configuration, then restarting sshd and rescanning.

scenario: The load average is high but CPU usage is low, and top shows high wa. What is the bottleneck?

options.text: Disk or storage I/O (processes waiting on I/O)

explanation: High load with low CPU and high wa in top means processes are waiting on disk or storage I/O. Use iostat -x, iotop or pidstat -d to find the busy device and process.

scenario: free shows almost no free memory but plenty "available." Is this a problem?

options.text: No; Linux uses spare RAM for cache and releases it when programs need it

explanation: Linux uses spare RAM for cache and releases it when programs need it, so low 'free' but healthy 'available' is normal. Watch swap activity (si/so in vmstat) and available instead.

scenario: A server swaps heavily and is slow. What should you check first?

options.text: Which processes use the most memory (top sorted by %MEM, or ps --sort=-rss)

explanation: For heavy swapping, find which processes use the most memory (top sorted by %MEM or ps --sort=-rss), then reduce usage, add RAM or tune vm.swappiness.

scenario: Which command shows the processes using the most CPU?
explanation: ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head (or top) shows the biggest CPU consumers. Then renice, limit with systemd CPUQuota= or stop the runaway process.

scenario: Which command collects performance data over time so you can compare with a baseline?
explanation: sar (from sysstat) records performance data over time, which lets you compare current behavior with a baseline. A single uptime reading gives no history.

scenario: An NFS mount is slow and processes hang in state D. What does D mean?

options.text: Uninterruptible sleep, usually waiting on I/O such as a storage or network file system

explanation: State D is uninterruptible sleep, usually waiting on I/O such as a storage or network file system like a slow NFS mount. Check network latency and the server's health.

scenario: After a GRUB configuration change, the system boots to a grub> prompt. What happened?

options.text: GRUB couldn't load its configuration or find the kernel; boot manually or rebuild grub.cfg from a rescue environment

explanation: A grub> prompt means GRUB couldn't load its configuration or find the kernel. Boot manually or, from rescue media, chroot and rebuild with grub2-mkconfig (and grub2-install on BIOS).

scenario: A new network card doesn't appear in ip link. What should you check?

options.text: Whether a driver is loaded: lspci -k and dmesg for errors, then load the module or install firmware

explanation: If a new NIC is missing from ip link, check whether its driver is loaded: lspci -k and dmesg for errors, then load the module or install firmware (some devices need non-free firmware packages).

scenario: Users report SSH connections take 30 seconds before the password prompt. What is a common cause?

options.text: The SSH server is doing slow reverse-DNS lookups (UseDNS) or GSSAPI attempts

explanation: A 30-second delay before the SSH password prompt is typically a slow reverse-DNS lookup (UseDNS) or GSSAPI attempt. Fix DNS or set UseDNS no and inspect with ssh -v.

scenario: A host on a dual-stack network can't reach a site that has both A and AAAA records. IPv4 works. What should you check?

options.text: IPv6 routing and firewall rules (ip -6 route, ping -6)

explanation: Clients prefer IPv6 when it's available, so a broken IPv6 path causes failures or delays while IPv4 works. Check ip -6 route, ping -6 and IPv6 firewall rules.

scenario: A cloud VM is unreachable after a reboot. What should you check first in the cloud console?

options.text: The serial console or boot logs and the security group or network ACL rules

options.note: You don't control them in public cloud.

explanation: For an unreachable cloud VM after a reboot, check the serial console or boot logs and the security group or network ACL rules. A bad fstab entry or firewall change is common; fix it from the serial console or by attaching the disk to another VM.
